clue.text: Scottish, might you say? That's funny!

indicators.note: asking what you might say points to a word judged by how it is spoken rather than spelt

parts.note: Jock is a nickname for a Scotsman, so a Jock-like manner would be Jock-ular

explanation.surface: Someone hears a Scottish accent and declares the result hilarious.
explanation.walkthrough: Jock is a common (slightly dated) British nickname for a Scot; the word for funny sounds like an adjective built from it.
explanation.definitionFit: Jocular describes speech or behaviour meant as a joke, so it is a ready synonym for humorous or amusing.

clue.text: Papers written up in project on hard book

indicators.note: in a down clue, on means placed above, so one piece sits before the next
in places one piece within the other

parts.note: to project is to stick out

indicators.note: in a down entry, written up means set upwards, so the papers are reversed

parts.note: ID is identity papers
H for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: Documents drafted for a project about a tough book.
explanation.definitionFit: Judith is a book of the Apocrypha, telling of the heroine who beheads Holofernes.

clue.text: Quick introduction to centrifugal force

indicators.note: an introduction is the opening, so only the first letter is kept

parts.note: the first letter of the word
to force open, prise

explanation.surface: A quick primer on centrifugal force, as in a physics lesson.
explanation.walkthrough: Force looks like the physics noun but is the verb, as in levering a lid open.
explanation.definitionFit: Quick can mean mentally sharp or bright, as in quick-witted, a synonym for intelligent.

clue.text: Party time under model coming up for Gilbert, perhaps?

indicators.note: under means placed below in a down entry, so time comes after the model

parts.note: LIB is short for Liberal, a political party

indicators.note: in a down entry, coming up means rising, so the model word is read bottom to top

parts.note: an artist's model is a sitter
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A party season under a rising model, perhaps on behalf of someone called Gilbert.
explanation.walkthrough: W S Gilbert wrote the words for Gilbert and Sullivan's comic operas; perhaps marks him as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Gilbert supplied the words for Sullivan's music, and the writer of an opera's text is its lyricist.

clue.text: On top, go over once more

parts.note: re means on, concerning
a cap is a lid or top

explanation.surface: An instruction: from the start, run through it all again.
explanation.definitionFit: To summarise the main points again is to review them a second time.

clue.text: Liberal, firm and good

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation for company, a firm
pious means devout, morally good

explanation.surface: A political description: a liberal, solid and virtuous figure.
explanation.walkthrough: Liberal looks like a political label, but here it means lavish or plentiful, as in a liberal helping.
explanation.definitionFit: A liberal amount is a generous, abundant one, and copious means plentiful in quantity.

clue.text: Cheat's character accidental

parts.note: a card is an eccentric character
in music an accidental is a sharp, flat or natural sign

explanation.surface: A cheat's personality is described as happening by chance.
explanation.walkthrough: Accidental looks like an adjective for chance, but it is the music noun for a sign raising or lowering a note.
explanation.definitionFit: A card sharp is a swindler who wins at gambling games by trickery and sleight of hand.

clue.text: Look, someone in the loo, so to speak?

indicators.note: speaking signals that the word is identified by its spoken sound

parts.note: a person in the toilet might be one who pees

explanation.surface: Glance over there: someone is in the toilet.
explanation.walkthrough: Loo is everyday British slang for a toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: To look closely or with difficulty, squinting at something, is a common verb sense.

clue.text: Paddle in doubt, struggling to find boat's motor

indicators.note: in places the paddle inside the reworked letters
something struggling is thrashing about, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
an oar is a paddle for rowing

explanation.surface: A rower struggles with a paddle, uncertain, wishing for a boat's engine.
explanation.definitionFit: An outboard is a detachable engine clamped to the stern of a small boat.

clue.text: Soldier crawling under material, seeing another soldier

indicators.note: under means placed below in a down entry, so the insect follows the material

parts.note: serge is a hard-wearing twilled cloth
a soldier ant is a crawling insect

explanation.surface: A soldier creeping beneath fabric spots a fellow serviceman.
explanation.walkthrough: The first soldier is an insect, a soldier ant, which is why it is crawling.
explanation.definitionFit: A sergeant is a non-commissioned army rank, so it names a further member of the forces.

clue.text: Schmuck we buried in plot, laid back

indicators.note: a thing buried in ground sits inside it, so one piece goes within the other
something laid back is turned the other way, so the plot word is read from its end

parts.note: a garden plot is a flower bed
taken as written

explanation.surface: An unpleasant man buried in a garden plot by a relaxed pair of conspirators.
explanation.walkthrough: Laid back sounds like a relaxed attitude but turns the plot round before the other word goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Schmuck is Yiddish-derived slang for a contemptible or foolish person, close to a nerdy, socially inept fool.

clue.text: President claims writer saw his tool?

indicators.note: to claim something is to take hold of it, so the president word wraps round the writer

parts.note: Jimmy Carter, US president 1977-81
a pen is a writing instrument

explanation.surface: A president insists a writer witnessed him with his implement.
explanation.walkthrough: Saw reads as the past of see, but it is the noun: a woodworker's cutting blade.
explanation.definitionFit: A woodworker who builds with timber uses a saw as a basic tool of the trade, hence the question mark.

clue.text: See 16
See 16
Bum on the floor, a fanatic hosting party

indicators.note: a host has guests inside, so the party goes within the fanatic

parts.note: someone knocked down is on the floor
taken as written
a nut is an enthusiast
a do is a party

explanation.surface: Someone sprawled on the floor, an enthusiast throwing a party.
explanation.walkthrough: Bum is the American sense, a vagrant, not the British backside.
explanation.definitionFit: A bum is a tramp or vagrant, and someone destitute and homeless is described as down-and-out.

clue.text: See 16
Person bound to come up with the goods in man's breakfast items

indicators.note: in a down entry, coming up means rising, so the bound person is read upwards

parts.note: a serf was a labourer bound to the land

indicators.note: in places the goods within the man's word

parts.note: man's read as he's, he is
G is good, so two of them are goods

explanation.surface: A dutiful person delivers what's needed for the man's breakfast.
explanation.walkthrough: To come up with the goods sounds like an idiom for delivering; it hides a reversal and the abbreviation GG.
explanation.definitionFit: Newly laid eggs, boiled or fried, are standard morning food, so they fit breakfast items.

clue.text: Old number 35 London bus we drove home to Scunthorpe, so luggage is all over the place!

indicators.note: luggage scattered all over the place is in disorder, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: the number spelt out as a word

parts.words: London bus we drove home to Scunthorpe, so luggage is
parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A trip home to Scunthorpe on a vintage London bus leaves the bags scattered everywhere.
explanation.walkthrough: Old number means an old song; 35 is spelt out, not a cross-reference. Scunthorpe is an English steel town in Lincolnshire.
explanation.definitionFit: The title is a 1959 novelty hit for Lonnie Donegan, a skiffle singer, so it is a vintage song.

clue.text: Vicar's right and always on target

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for right
ever means always
an end is an aim or target

explanation.surface: A vicar is correct and never misses his aim.
explanation.walkthrough: On means placed after here, the down entry stacking the aim beneath.
explanation.definitionFit: Reverend is the courtesy title of a clergyman, used informally as a noun for a parish priest.

clue.text: 11 pigs or bats rising late

indicators.note: bats means crazy, so the letters before it are thrown into disorder

parts.note: the number spelt out as a word
taken as written

explanation.surface: A list of creatures — eleven pigs or bats — climbing into the air at a late hour.
explanation.walkthrough: The 11 is not a cross-reference to another clue but the number spelt in letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting up from bed later than intended is what happens when you sleep past the alarm.

clue.text: In fleeting instant, pointing to the sky for light

indicators.note: in a down entry, pointing skyward means running upwards, so the letters read in reverse
in says the letters lie inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters spanning the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: A flash of a moment, aimed upwards, like a firework being set off.
explanation.definitionFit: To light a fire or fuse is to set it burning, a verb synonym for kindle.

clue.text: Dirt's ending underneath a shoe — that's charming

definitions.note: a phrase for a thing that charms; the answer is a noun

indicators.note: underneath means placed below in a down entry, so that letter comes last

parts.note: taken as written
a mule is a backless slipper or shoe

indicators.note: the ending of a word is its last letter, which alone is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: Muck on the bottom of a shoe — how lovely, says someone sarcastically.
explanation.walkthrough: That's charming! is usually sarcastic; here it literally means a thing that works a charm.
explanation.definitionFit: An amulet is a trinket worn to ward off evil, a lucky charm with magic power.

clue.text: Look, someone in a turban, so to speak?

indicators.note: speaking signals that the word is identified by its spoken sound

parts.note: a male Sikh traditionally wears a turban

explanation.surface: Glance over there: a man wearing a turban.
explanation.definitionFit: To look for something is to search or hunt for it, a common verb sense.

clue.text: See 16
Fighting to curb tide, I'd lost — to this?

definitions.text: Fighting to curb tide, I'd lost — to this?

indicators.note: to curb is to restrain or hem in, so the fighting word goes round

parts.note: war is fighting

indicators.note: lost says those two letters go missing from the word before

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, the letters to remove

explanation.surface: Someone who battled the tide admits defeat — to the sea itself?
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue doubles as the definition: what a person fighting a tide loses to is the sea it is made of.
explanation.definitionFit: A tide is the rise and fall of the sea, so anyone losing that battle is beaten by the liquid itself.

clue.text: Monarch born, one wounded in massacre

parts.note: K is the abbreviation for king
née means born, used before a maiden name

explanation.surface: A king is born, and one person is injured in a slaughter.
explanation.walkthrough: Wounded Knee, South Dakota, was the site of the 1890 massacre of Lakota people by US troops.
explanation.definitionFit: The joint's name joins the word wounded in Wounded Knee, the site of a notorious massacre.

clue.text: See 16
College opening

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a college of Oxford University
second meaning: a projecting bay window

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as a college's inauguration; instead it is an Oxford college and a kind of window.
explanation.definitionFit: Oriel names both an Oxford college and an upper-storey bay window, a window being an opening in a wall.

clue.text: Reserves stuffing Manchester United, perhaps? Correct

indicators.note: stuffing goes inside a bird, so the reserves piece is packed into the team

parts.note: the Reds is Manchester United's nickname, from their red shirts; perhaps marks it as one example
RES is the abbreviation for reserves

explanation.surface: A football manager bolsters Manchester United with reserve players to put things right.
explanation.walkthrough: Several clubs are called the Reds, hence 'perhaps'.
explanation.definitionFit: To redress a wrong or imbalance is to put it right, so it is a verb synonym for correct.

clue.text: Leave handle again?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to withdraw or pull back
second meaning: read as RE- plus treat, to deal with a second time

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the split reading: re-treat, treating once more.
explanation.definitionFit: An army withdrawing pulls back from a position, and splitting the word gives treat a second time.
